lines.text: There are really only two ways anyone has ever built full serializability. Here's the first.
Lock whatever you touch, and don't let go until you commit. Anyone who wants the same data has to wait their turn.
If two transactions end up waiting on each other, that's a deadlock, and one of them gets rolled back to break it.
Here's the second way, and it looks nothing like the first.
Run snapshot isolation exactly the way it already runs. Nothing blocks. Nobody waits for anybody.
The only new thing is a watcher, checking the read write conflicts between transactions that are running at the same time.
Both of these actually deliver the exact same guarantee, full serializability, no exceptions.
Here's my prediction.
Locking blocks you up front. Watching lets you run and sometimes throws your work away afterward. Does that cost the same either way?
It really doesn't, and the measurements in this topic are going to make that concrete, not just plausible.
One route makes you wait before you've done any work. The other lets you do the work and sometimes wastes it.
Same promise. Two genuinely different bills.
So what exactly is that watcher looking for? One specific shape.
Two transactions, each reading data the other one is about to write, chained together through a transaction sitting in the middle.
That chain, two read write conflicts back to back, is the one pattern every single write skew anomaly turns out to have.

lines.text: Now watch it actually happen, against a real table, not a diagram.
I ran the exact same doctors scenario from last topic, with nothing changed except the isolation level.
One doctor's commit goes through clean. The other one gets handed a real serialization failure, straight from the engine.
That failed transaction doesn't just disappear. It's supposed to try again, and I built exactly that.
The retry starts completely fresh, with a brand new snapshot of the actual current data.
This time the count it reads is the real one, the other doctor already left, and it correctly decides to stay.
So here's the actual price tag on each side, stated plainly.
Locking makes you wait, and under real contention it can tip into a deadlock that rolls someone back anyway.
Watching never makes you wait at all, but it will sometimes cancel a transaction that was never actually going to cause a problem.
I didn't just state that false positive cost, I measured it, at two different levels of contention.
With two transactions sharing one rule, about half of them get aborted.
Scale that up to six transactions sharing the exact same rule, and most of them get aborted. The rate climbs, for real, as the crowd grows.
Put the two routes side by side.
One guarantee, full serializability, reached two completely different ways.
One of them bills you in blocking and the occasional deadlock. The other bills you in false alarms and mandatory retries.

lines.text: Last one. Picture a workload where most of the contention lands on just a handful of very hot rows.
Given everything you just watched, which of these two routes handles that better, locking or watching?
Think about where each one's own real cost actually gets worse as things get busier.
It's tempting to reach for the one that never blocks, since that sounds strictly better on paper.
But the watcher's own false positive rate climbs fastest exactly where reads and writes overlap the most, and a few very hot rows is exactly that.
Strict locking's blocking is at least predictable there. For this specific shape of contention, that's usually the better trade.
